primary_sources: Theodore Gentilz, Fall of the Alamo, 1844

stimulus.text: Theodore Gentilz painted this scene of the fall of the Alamo in 1844, eight years after the battle. The Alamo mission compound stands behind a wide open plain, and rows of soldiers stand in formation in the foreground.
stimulus.source_note: Painting viewed before writing: Theodore Gentilz, Fall of the Alamo, 1844, shared pool file u4/5s24-ch03-mcq-39.jpg, public domain. Gentilz painted the 1836 battle eight years after it happened; he was not an eyewitness.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Theodore Gentilz, Fall of the Alamo, 1844, public domain
stem: The battle shown in the painting ended in defeat for the Texan defenders. What followed it in 1836?

options.text: Mexico reconquered Texas after the Alamo and ended the rebellion for good
options.misconception: Mexico won at the Alamo but lost the war weeks later at San Jacinto.

options.text: Texan forces under Sam Houston won independence at San Jacinto
The United States annexed Texas at once
options.misconception: Annexation waited until 1845; Texas first stood as an independent republic.

options.text: Texas abolished slavery and joined Mexico again
options.misconception: Texas kept slavery and became independent; it did not rejoin Mexico.

rationales.A: Mexico won at the Alamo but lost the war weeks later at San Jacinto.
rationales.B: Houston regrouped after the Alamo and defeated the Mexican army at San Jacinto, and Texas became an independent republic in 1836.
rationales.C: Annexation waited until 1845. Texas first stood as an independent republic.
rationales.D: Texas kept slavery and became independent. It did not rejoin Mexico.
rationales.general:
1. Note the defeat. The Alamo fell in March 1836, and almost 200 defenders died.
2. Ask what came next. Sam Houston regrouped the Texan army and won at San Jacinto that April.
3. Name the result. The victory made Texas an independent republic, not a Mexican province.
Background: The battle cry after the Alamo was to remember it, and San Jacinto answered it.
Remember: one battle can lose while the war is still won.
